newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's Tudjman in democracy test.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Tudjman in democracy test.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman will have a chance to show democracy is more solid in Croatia than in Serbia -- ruled by his old nemesis Slobodan Milosevic -- when Croats vote this spring in regional elections.

Tudjman's nationalist HDZ party, its popularity declining over bread-and-butter issues, could be beaten by opposition coalitions in key municipalities in the April 13 elections, which were formally announced on Wednesday.

The question is whether the HDZ will readily accept defeat, especially in the capital Zagreb, unlike Milosevic's Serbian Socialists who admitted losing November municipal elections this week only after three months of mass opposition protests.

For Tudjman to prove his claim that Croatia belongs to the West while Serbia, its former rival in old federal Yugoslavia, is "Balkan" and anti-democratic, will take no less than the HDZ ceding power for the first time since winning it in 1990.

Tudjman and his Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) has won virtually every election held in Croatia since the first free vote that heralded the fall of communism in 1990, the year before Yugoslavia's breakup.
But recent opinion polls show that the April 13 elections might prove the toughest test for the HDZ ever.

An extensive countrywide poll in the independent weekly Nacional published on Tuesday showed that if the elections were held today, the HDZ would finish second behind a centrist coalition in most regions.
Political analysts have debated how Tudjman, 74, a former communist general with autocratic tendencies, will react in the case of a possible, if not probable, HDZ defeat.

On the only occasion where Tudjman should have relinquished significant HDZ power -- after his party lost regional voting in Zagreb in 1995 -- he failed the test of democracy by using his constitutional "national security" authority to block the appointment of opposition candidates for mayor.
Zagreb remains under provisional HDZ rule today.

"Tudjman is confident that the HDZ would win the upcoming elections but he told (the U.S. television network) CNN that he would respect the results whatever they might turn out to be," a Western diplomat said.
"I would be very surprised if he did not relinquish power in case of a defeat. Tudjman knows that the consequences would be disastrous," the diplomat told Reuters.
Croatia would find itself immediately isolated from the international community and its financial resources, which would hit its restructuring economy hard, diplomats said.

Any serious rigging or annulment of election results could well trigger mass protests of the kind that have been shaking Serbia -- from which Croatia likes to distance itself -- for three months, analysts said.

Mass demonstrations in Zagreb last November, when 100,000 people protested over a state attempt to close an independent radio station, showed that Croatia's political scene contains similar potential for an anti-government eruption.

Some analysts feel Tudjman would not accept opposition victories where they would most damage him. But in this case, they say, he would manipulate the political process in more subtle ways than in Serbia to avert mass protests.

"Tudjman would never accept opposition victories in key counties, including Zagreb. But he will not play the same game as Milosevic -- to steal elections openly," said Davor Gjenero, a leading Croatian political observer.
He said Tudjman could always use his constitutional power to approve county heads and the mayor of Zagreb to prevent the opposition from taking power in key areas.
"A protracted process would not irritate the public as an outright open fraud (as in Serbia)," Gjenero said.

Tudjman could resort to stalling tactics until presidential elections this summer which he is widely tipped to win in the absence of charismatic challengers, giving him a new term in office to re-bolster HDZ rule at local levels.
Tudjman recently announced he would run for another term despite reportedly suffering stomach cancer which appears to have gone into remission after extended treatment.
